item: A re-index writes only the mention rows that changed, and the drain reports what it kept, updated, removed and added
summary: Lenovo's drain ran at 7,673 articles an hour (2.1 a second) because every re-indexed article deleted and re-inserted about 80 mention rows through ten indexes in a 41 GB encrypted file. index_article now reads the article's rows once and writes the difference: an unchanged row keeps its id and created_at, a changed row is updated in place under its id and stamped now, a gone row is deleted, a new one inserted; every stored column but identity and write time is compared. The drain's stats gain rows kept, updated, removed and added and a split of the apply time. The old rows are read inside the write window, so another writer cannot leave the diff working from rows that no longer exist. A drain that walked a batch ends with its corpus-epoch bump BEFORE the whole-corpus counter sweep (and again after one that reconciled), so a kill inside the sweep no longer skips it. The write-rate diagnostic's caveat now says it counts rows written, so its articles per hour is a lower bound. The speed-up is a best case: on a sandbox pass where every row was unchanged the mention SQL fell from 9.5 s to 1.1 s; articles with no stored rows (option-(a) imports) save nothing, and rows an older engine wrote often differ and are updated; the drain stats show the real split.
